segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Chapter 4. The Bramdean Road.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The scheme was Mrs Pike's and she thought it could not be improved upon. Fenner the mason would not put a figure on paper for anybody who did not come and stand in his yard, and Bramdean is six miles, and Mr Rowe had the loan of the Ludds' donkey cart on a Friday. A young lady who had asked how many children there were in the parish would naturally wish to hear what a roof cost.

segments.speaker: Mrs Honoria Pike
segments.text: Six miles out and six back, and nothing to do the whole way but talk. I have never known it fail.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On the Friday morning the gatehouse maid came down with a note. Miss Marchmont was writing to her uncle, was at her fourth sheet, and could not go to Bramdean nor anywhere else until the post went out on Tuesday.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Mrs Pike read this on her own doorstep with the cart already standing at the gate, and Miss Vane came across the green at that moment with a basket, going up to the draper's for black thread and tape.

segments.speaker: Mrs Honoria Pike
segments.text: Miss Vane. You are walking anyway. Go with him and see the figure written down and the man's name under it, for the curate will come home with the sum in his head and forget the shillings.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: I am going for thread.

segments.speaker: Mrs Honoria Pike
segments.text: Thread will keep. Four sheets to her uncle, and she has been down here a week. Four sheets is not a letter about damp, whatever she says.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She was still turning the note over when the cart went off up the lane, and it did not occur to her then, or for some hours afterwards, that there was nobody in it but the two of them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: A mile past the mill the near wheel went into a rut it had gone into fifty times before, and the felloe split from the spoke outward with a noise like a hurdle breaking. The cart sat down on its axle. The donkey stopped and stood, quite unbothered, and Mr Rowe got him out of the shafts and tied him to the hedge, and there was nothing else whatever to be done until somebody came along the road.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They sat on the verge. It was a quarter of an hour before either of them said anything that was not about the wheel.

segments.speaker: Mr Silas Rowe
segments.text: It was Chronicles.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: It was.

segments.speaker: Mr Silas Rowe
segments.text: I have carried that morning about with me since November. In my account of it there were six people in the room and every one of them heard you, and one of the Barrow girls laughed.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: There were four of us and nobody laughed. You had said it twice already and you were going to the visitation on the Thursday. I thought it kinder to say it in front of Mrs Hale than to let you say it in front of the archdeacon.

segments.speaker: Mr Silas Rowe
segments.text: That is kinder. I did not think of it as kindness at the time.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: I have a list of six books that came back into my hand on the green in October. You had not read one of them.

segments.speaker: Mr Silas Rowe
segments.text: I had not read one of them. I knew it while I was handing it back, and I was ashamed of the word I used before I reached the lych gate, and I have never once said so out loud until this minute.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: Trash.

segments.speaker: Mr Silas Rowe
segments.text: Trash. Mrs Cobbe lay there till February looking at a ceiling and I gave her back the list.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Judith looked at the road, which stayed empty. In her own account of that morning he had smiled while he said it. He had not smiled. She had put the smile in herself, somewhere about Christmas, and had kept it there because it made the thing easier to hold.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: We have neither of us been telling it straight.

segments.speaker: Mr Silas Rowe
segments.text: No. Mine had grown a good deal in the keeping.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It was the better part of an hour before Nye came by with a load of hurdles and room for two on the board. He set the wheel on the top of the load, and led the donkey behind, and did not hurry his horse for anybody, and the sun was well down over the Alresford road before the first cottages showed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Judith was laughing as they came in, at something he had said about Fenner's yard dog, and she was still laughing when the cart came round the corner of the green.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The green was not empty. It was Friday, and the London coach stood outside the Bell with its lamps lit and half the parish about it, and above the draper's the library window was bright, and Mrs Hale was standing in it with her spectacles pushed up into her hair.
